title: Herbal and Supplement Interactions: Natural Does Not Mean Interaction-Free
bottomLine: Treat natural health products as active therapies. Ask specifically about vitamins, minerals, herbal products and traditional/complementary remedies; verify Canadian authorization and known interaction or pregnancy risks; and never assume a product is safe because it is sold without a prescription.
recognize: Natural health products can alter bleeding, sedation, blood pressure, glucose and drug metabolism.
Product quality, ingredient concentration and evidence vary; an NPN indicates authorization, not proof that the product is appropriate for every patient.
differentiate: Traditional or culturally important product use should be discussed respectfully rather than dismissed.
A suspected interaction requires assessment of timing, dose, competing causes and the prescription drug's therapeutic index.
assessment: Ask product name/brand, ingredients, dose, reason for use, duration, pregnancy/breastfeeding, surgery plans and all prescription/OTC medications.
workup: Use product-specific evidence and targeted INR, glucose, BP, liver/renal or drug-level monitoring only when the suspected interaction warrants it.
management: Stop or substitute a product when interaction risk outweighs benefit; coordinate with pharmacist/specialist for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs or uncertain high-risk combinations.
medicationSafety: Extra caution is required with anticoagulants, sedatives, transplant/immunosuppressive therapy and pregnancy; unlicensed online products may contain undeclared ingredients.
redFlags: Pregnancy exposure to an unsafe product
counselling: Encourage patients to bring product containers/photos and to check before starting or stopping supplements.
followUp: Reassess symptoms and relevant monitoring after discontinuing or changing an interacting product.
examTrap: Ignoring a supplement because it is 'natural' while troubleshooting unexplained bleeding or drug toxicity.
oneLinePearl: Natural products belong on the medication list because they can change medication outcomes.
sourceBasis: Health Canada natural health product safety and interaction resources

title: Medication Reconciliation: One Accurate List, One Explained Plan
bottomLine: Medication reconciliation compares the best possible medication history with the intended current regimen and resolves every discrepancy. It is not copying the old medication list forward; each drug must be continued, changed or stopped deliberately with ownership and patient understanding.
recognize: Transitions, multiple prescribers, cognitive impairment and incomplete pharmacy records create high discrepancy risk.
Omissions, duplicates, wrong doses and failure to restart intentionally held medications can all cause harm.
differentiate: Reconciliation establishes what the patient actually takes; medication review decides what they should take.
A discrepancy can be intentional, but it still requires documentation.
assessment: Use patient/caregiver interview plus containers, pharmacy/dispensing records and recent discharge/specialist lists; include OTC/natural products and actual adherence.
workup: Check labs or levels only when a discrepancy may already have caused toxicity or loss of control.
management: Resolve each discrepancy with the appropriate prescriber/pharmacist, document the final regimen and communicate it to the patient and next care setting.
medicationSafety: High-alert drugs, anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, steroids, immunosuppressants and antiseizure drugs deserve particular transition attention.
redFlags: Missing basal insulin in type 1 diabetes
counselling: Provide a clear updated list with what changed and why; use teach-back.
followUp: Assign ownership for pending monitoring and confirm the reconciled list reaches community clinicians/pharmacy.
examTrap: Calling reconciliation complete because the electronic medication list was imported without asking what the patient actually takes.
oneLinePearl: Reconciliation turns multiple medication lists into one intentional plan.
sourceBasis: College of Nurses of Ontario documentation and medication standards

title: Prescribing in Pregnancy and Lactation: Treat the Patient and the Exposure Context
bottomLine: Medication decisions in pregnancy and lactation balance the risk of treatment, the risk of untreated disease, gestational or infant age, dose/route and available alternatives. Do not abruptly stop effective necessary therapy simply because pregnancy or breastfeeding begins.
recognize: Teratogenic risk differs by drug and timing; breastfeeding exposure depends on milk transfer, infant absorption and infant vulnerability.
Untreated epilepsy, severe mental illness, hypertension, infection or diabetes can itself create major maternal/fetal risk.
differentiate: Pregnancy risk is not captured by an old letter category or one internet list.
A drug contraindicated in pregnancy may have a different lactation profile and vice versa.
assessment: Confirm pregnancy/lactation status and timing, indication/severity, prior response, dose/route, alternatives, maternal organ function and infant gestational age/health when breastfeeding.
workup: Use current Canadian product monograph and condition-specific obstetric/lactation resources; obtain drug-specific monitoring when required.
management: Continue, switch, dose-adjust or stop according to individualized benefit-risk; involve obstetric/pediatric/specialty expertise for high-risk drugs or severe disease.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors/ARBs and selected teratogens require pregnancy-specific action; valproate and other high-risk drugs require specialist reproductive planning.
redFlags: Maternal disease destabilization after abrupt discontinuation
Medication essential to prevent maternal crisis
counselling: Discuss risks of both medication and untreated disease in absolute, non-alarmist terms.
followUp: Reassess as pregnancy stage, delivery, breastfeeding and maternal disease change.
examTrap: Automatically stopping a stable essential medication when pregnancy is confirmed without assessing relapse or disease risk.
oneLinePearl: Pregnancy prescribing compares two risks: treatment and untreated illness.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada guidance

title: Pediatric Prescribing: Weight, Age, Formulation, Maximum Dose, Caregiver Safety
bottomLine: Children are not small adults. Confirm current weight, age/gestation, indication, formulation concentration, organ function and dose ceiling; calculate and independently recheck weight-based dosing, then give caregivers an unambiguous volume/device plan.
recognize: Developmental pharmacokinetics, changing weight and liquid concentrations create unique error risk.
OTC products and combination cough/cold medicines can create duplicate ingredients and age-specific hazards.
differentiate: A mathematically correct mg/kg dose can still exceed the recommended maximum adult/condition dose.
Milligrams and millilitres are not interchangeable.
assessment: Record measured current weight in kilograms, allergies, renal/hepatic status, age, swallowing/formulation needs and caregiver health literacy.
workup: Use current pediatric monograph/formulary guidance and drug-specific monitoring; do not extrapolate adult dosing when pediatric evidence differs.
management: Calculate mg/kg or body-surface-area dosing only when appropriate, apply maximum limits, specify concentration and mL per dose, and use standardized oral syringes/devices.
medicationSafety: Avoid decimal/trailing-zero errors, household-spoon dosing and duplicate acetaminophen/other active ingredients across products.
redFlags: Caregiver unable to reproduce the dosing plan
counselling: Have the caregiver demonstrate dose measurement and explain interval/max daily dosing.
followUp: Recalculate when weight or organ function changes during prolonged therapy.
examTrap: Converting a weight-based milligram dose to millilitres without checking the product concentration or maximum dose.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric prescribing requires weight, concentration and maximum-dose checks every time.
sourceBasis: Health Canada pediatric medication safety resources

title: Geriatric Prescribing: Function, Frailty, Renal Clearance, Falls, Time to Benefit
bottomLine: Prescribe for the older adult's physiology, function and goals—not chronological age. Review renal function, frailty, cognition, falls/orthostasis, anticholinergic/sedative burden, time to benefit and treatment burden before adding or intensifying therapy.
recognize: Adverse effects may present as falls, delirium, constipation, incontinence, anorexia or functional decline.
Preventive treatment benefit may take longer than the patient's realistic horizon or may still be highly valuable when function/life expectancy support it.
differentiate: Many medications can be appropriate despite age; the target is inappropriate burden, not an arbitrary drug count.
Frailty is not synonymous with age or dementia.
assessment: Review goals, ADLs/IADLs, cognition, falls/orthostasis, renal/hepatic function, swallowing, adherence, caregiver support and complete medication list.
workup: Use drug-specific monitoring and reassess renal function during acute illness; review whether a new symptom may be medication-related before adding another drug.
management: Use the lowest treatment burden that achieves meaningful outcomes, deprescribe low-benefit/high-harm therapy and taper dependence/rebound-prone drugs safely.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, sedatives, hypoglycemia-causing agents, NSAIDs, anticoagulants and hypotensive combinations deserve individualized risk review.
counselling: Discuss tradeoffs among symptom relief, prevention, independence and treatment burden.
followUp: Track function and adverse effects after changes, not laboratory targets alone.
examTrap: Adding another medication for dizziness/constipation/confusion without reviewing whether the current regimen caused it.
oneLinePearl: In geriatrics, medication success includes preserved function and fewer harms.

title: Medication Adherence: Diagnose the Barrier Before Adding More Medicine
bottomLine: When treatment appears ineffective, ask how the medication is actually being used before escalating. Adherence barriers may be cost, access, adverse effects, complexity, cognition, beliefs, language, unstable housing, swallowing or misunderstanding; the intervention must match the barrier.
recognize: Nonadherence is often rational from the patient's perspective and may be hidden by shame or fear of judgment.
Complex schedules and frequent refills create avoidable failure even when motivation is high.
differentiate: Intentional nonadherence from adverse effects or beliefs differs from unintentional forgetfulness/access barriers.
A refill record estimates acquisition, not ingestion.
assessment: Ask nonjudgmentally about missed doses, cost/coverage, side effects, routine, literacy/language, cognition, caregiver support, substance use and goals.
workup: Use objective disease markers or drug levels only when clinically meaningful; do not use testing punitively.
management: Simplify regimen, synchronize refills, use blister packs/reminders, address adverse effects/cost, use interpretation and involve supports with consent.
medicationSafety: Do not intensify high-risk therapy until you know whether the current regimen is being taken; restarting after a long gap may require retitration for some drugs.
counselling: Normalize adherence difficulties and build the plan with the patient rather than assigning blame.
followUp: Reassess the identified barrier and clinical outcome after the intervention.
examTrap: Adding a second antihypertensive when the patient has not filled the first because of cost.
oneLinePearl: Before escalating therapy, find out whether the current therapy reached the patient.

title: Cost-Effective Prescribing: Highest Value, Not Cheapest Sticker Price
bottomLine: Cost-effective prescribing chooses the option with the best expected benefit, harm, adherence and total resource use for the patient—not simply the lowest acquisition price. Provincial/territorial formularies and coverage vary, so access must be checked before finalizing a plan.
recognize: A cheaper drug that causes nonadherence, monitoring burden or preventable complications may be poor value.
Generic or formulary-preferred options can offer equivalent benefit when clinically appropriate.
differentiate: Cost-effectiveness is not rationing by income and does not justify withholding clearly superior necessary therapy.
Public coverage criteria differ from clinical indication.
assessment: Assess indication, comparative efficacy/safety, monitoring, dosing complexity, coverage, out-of-pocket cost, transportation and patient priorities.
workup: Check provincial/territorial formulary and special-authorization requirements when relevant rather than assuming Canada-wide coverage.
management: Choose evidence-supported lower-burden options when equivalent, reduce unnecessary duplication/testing and help navigate coverage for higher-value therapies when justified.
medicationSafety: Do not switch stable narrow-index or formulation-sensitive therapy solely for cost without evaluating equivalence and monitoring needs.
redFlags: Coverage delay causing dangerous treatment interruption
Cost-driven substitution with clinically nonequivalent therapy
counselling: Discuss cost directly and transparently; offer choices without shame.
followUp: Confirm the prescription was actually obtained and remains affordable.
examTrap: Calling the cheapest medication the most cost-effective when it creates poor adherence or inferior outcomes.
oneLinePearl: Value includes outcomes, harms, burden and access—not just price.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada high-value care principles

title: Electronic Prescribing: Structured Orders Still Need Clinical Verification
bottomLine: Electronic prescribing reduces some handwriting/transmission errors but creates new risks such as wrong-patient selection, default doses, duplicate orders, autopopulated directions and alert fatigue. Verify patient, drug, dose, units, route, frequency, duration, indication and destination pharmacy before signing.
recognize: Copied orders and defaults can perpetuate outdated renal dosing or discontinued therapy.
Alert fatigue can cause clinicians to override both low-value and genuinely dangerous warnings.
differentiate: A successful electronic transmission does not prove the pharmacy received an intentional, clinically correct prescription.
Clinical decision support assists judgment; it does not replace it.
assessment: Confirm patient identifiers, allergies, medication list, current organ function, pharmacy and the indication being treated.
workup: Use audit/medication history and pharmacy clarification when an electronic discrepancy is suspected.
management: Use standardized sigs and units, avoid unsafe abbreviations, discontinue obsolete orders rather than simply adding replacements, and communicate urgent corrections directly.
medicationSafety: High-risk e-prescribing errors include insulin concentration, methotrexate frequency, anticoagulant duplication, pediatric decimal/weight errors and wrong formulation.
redFlags: Prescription sent to wrong pharmacy with urgent drug
counselling: Give the patient the medication name/purpose so they can detect dispensing discrepancies.
followUp: Confirm urgent prescriptions and critical corrections were received and acted on.
examTrap: Assuming the EHR's default dose is correct because no hard-stop alert appeared.
oneLinePearl: Electronic prescribing changes the error types; it does not eliminate verification.

title: Prescription Error Prevention: Design the Order So Misinterpretation Is Hard
bottomLine: Prevent prescribing errors by making the intended therapy explicit and independently checking high-risk calculations. Use metric units, leading zeros, no trailing zeros, complete directions and indication when helpful; eliminate ambiguous abbreviations and reconcile duplicate or discontinued orders.
recognize: Dose/decimal, unit, frequency, formulation, route and duplicate-therapy errors are predictable system hazards.
Verbal orders and transitions increase risk when read-back or documentation is incomplete.
differentiate: An error caught before reaching the patient is still a safety signal worth learning from.
Human vigilance alone is weaker than standardization, forcing functions and independent checks for high-risk processes.
assessment: Before signing, verify patient, indication, allergies, drug, formulation/concentration, dose calculation, route, frequency, duration and relevant organ function.
workup: If an error reached the patient, assess actual exposure and obtain poison-centre/specialty or clinical monitoring according to the drug.
management: Correct the prescription, communicate directly with pharmacy/patient when time-sensitive, disclose/manage patient harm appropriately and use the incident to improve the system.
medicationSafety: Independent double checks are particularly important for weight-based pediatrics, insulin, anticoagulants, chemotherapy and other high-alert medications.
counselling: Encourage patients to ask when a medication looks different or the directions do not match what was discussed.
followUp: Close the loop on corrections and monitor for delayed harm.
examTrap: Fixing the EHR order but failing to tell the pharmacy that the already-transmitted erroneous prescription must be cancelled.
oneLinePearl: A safe order is hard to misread and easy to verify.
sourceBasis: Canadian medication incident and patient-safety principles
Health Canada safe medication use resources

title: High-Alert Medication Safety: Small Error, Disproportionate Harm
bottomLine: High-alert medications require stronger systems because ordinary errors can cause catastrophic harm. Standardize concentrations/processes, verify indication and patient-specific dose, use independent checks when appropriate, monitor for predictable toxicity and make reversal/rescue plans accessible.
recognize: Insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, chemotherapy, concentrated electrolytes and other high-risk therapies can cause severe harm from relatively small deviations.
Look-alike packaging, unit confusion and infusion-programming errors amplify risk.
differentiate: High-alert does not mean avoid the medication; it means add risk controls.
A double check should be independent and meaningful rather than ceremonial co-signing.
assessment: Confirm indication, patient identity, allergies, weight/organ function, concentration, dose/units, route, interactions and recent monitoring.
workup: Use drug-specific labs/levels, ECG, glucose or other monitoring according to the therapy.
management: Apply standardized order sets/concentrations, independent verification, smart-pump/other safeguards and clear escalation/reversal protocols where applicable.
medicationSafety: Never use ambiguous insulin units, unsafe decimal notation or unreviewed duplicate anticoagulation; separate/constrain concentrated products according to organizational policy.
counselling: Teach patient-specific warning symptoms and rescue actions such as glucagon or naloxone where appropriate.
followUp: Audit near misses and actual events for system fixes, not only individual blame.
examTrap: Treating a high-alert medication like any routine prescription because the calculated dose is technically correct.
sourceBasis: Canadian medication-safety and high-alert medication principles

title: Transdermal and Injectable Medications: Route Changes Pharmacology and Error Risk
bottomLine: Route and formulation are part of the drug. Transdermal systems can continue releasing medication after application and are affected by skin/heat; injectable products differ by concentration, device, route and technique. Never substitute formulation or route from name alone.
recognize: Patches can be missed during reconciliation and may cause duplicate dosing if the old patch is not removed.
Injectables carry concentration, needle/device, site and storage risks.
differentiate: Immediate-release, depot/long-acting, pen, vial, autoinjector and patch formulations are not dose-equivalent by assumption.
Crushing/opening or cutting a delivery system can alter release and exposure.
assessment: Confirm exact product/formulation/concentration, route, site, timing, skin integrity, device competence and storage requirements.
workup: Use therapy-specific monitoring and assess injection-site or absorption problems when efficacy/toxicity is unexpected.
management: Teach correct site rotation, patch removal/application timing, injection preparation/device use and sharps disposal; verify any formulation conversion using current monograph guidance.
medicationSafety: External heat can increase absorption for some patches; long-acting injectable errors may persist for weeks and require urgent specialist advice.
redFlags: Depot medication given by wrong route
counselling: Have the patient demonstrate device/patch technique and explain storage/disposal.
followUp: Review sites, technique, adherence and formulation at transitions.
examTrap: Applying a new patch without checking whether the old patch is still present.
oneLinePearl: With patches and injectables, formulation and route are part of the dose.
sourceBasis: Canadian medication administration and sharps safety principles

title: Compounded Medications: Individualized Need, Quality, Stability, Traceability
bottomLine: Compounding is justified by an individual clinical need when an appropriate authorized commercial product is unavailable or unsuitable; it is not routine manufacturing or a way to bypass approved products. The prescriber must ensure a clear formulation, strength, route, stability/beyond-use plan, monitoring and a qualified pharmacy/compounder under applicable provincial or territorial standards.
recognize: Compounded products may have different stability, bioavailability and error risk from commercial products.
Children, allergy/excipient intolerance, swallowing limitations or unavailable strengths can create legitimate individualized need.
differentiate: Compounding and manufacturing have different regulatory responsibilities.
A compounded product should not be assumed equivalent to an authorized commercial product without supporting evidence.
assessment: Document why commercial options are unsuitable, exact active ingredients/strength/vehicle/route, allergies, organ function and ability to measure/administer the formulation.
workup: Verify formulation evidence, compatibility/stability and monitoring with pharmacist/compounder; use current provincial/territorial standards.
management: Write an unambiguous prescription and coordinate with a qualified compounding pharmacy; communicate concentration and beyond-use/storage requirements to patient/caregiver.
medicationSafety: Concentration errors can cause major pediatric or narrow-index overdoses; avoid vague instructions such as 'compound as usual'.
redFlags: Compounded alternative replacing an appropriate authorized product without rationale
counselling: Explain that compounded products require specific storage, measuring devices and expiry/beyond-use instructions.
followUp: Reassess efficacy, adverse effects and whether an authorized product has become available.
examTrap: Assuming any requested compounded concentration is safe because a pharmacy can technically prepare it.
oneLinePearl: Compounding solves an individual formulation problem; it creates extra quality and dosing responsibilities.
sourceBasis: Health Canada manufacturing and compounding policies
Provincial and territorial pharmacy compounding standards

title: Medication Storage and Stability: Potency and Safety Depend on Conditions
bottomLine: Follow product-specific labeled storage and transportation conditions. Heat, freezing, light, moisture, contamination, time after opening/reconstitution and cold-chain interruption can reduce potency or safety; do not guess that a medication is usable after an excursion.
recognize: Insulin, biologics, vaccines, reconstituted antibiotics, eye drops and compounded products may have important temperature/time constraints.
Bathroom cabinets, hot cars and freezing exposure are common home storage problems.
differentiate: Manufacturer expiry date and beyond-use time after opening/reconstitution are different concepts.
A product that looks normal may still have lost potency after an unacceptable temperature excursion.
assessment: Confirm exact product, storage history, time opened/reconstituted, temperature/light exposure, device integrity and contamination risk.
workup: Check current product monograph/manufacturer or pharmacist stability information for excursions rather than extrapolating from another formulation.
management: Replace/discard products when stability cannot be assured, maintain cold chain where required and provide written storage/transport instructions.
medicationSafety: Do not freeze products that must be refrigerated unless explicitly permitted; do not use damaged, contaminated or improperly stored injectable products.
redFlags: Reconstituted medication beyond validated use period
Unknown excursion for a critical narrow-index therapy
counselling: Teach where to store the product, travel/cold-chain planning, disposal, and what to do after a suspected excursion.
followUp: If reduced potency may have affected treatment or immunization, reassess clinical protection/control and follow product/program guidance.
examTrap: Using a refrigerated medication after it froze because the vial still looks normal.
oneLinePearl: Medication quality is part of the dose; storage conditions preserve the intended therapy.
sourceBasis: Health Canada drug storage and transportation guidance
